prompt.context: You are having lunch with the CEO of a major furniture manufacturer (couches, loveseats, and tables). He shows you the income statement for their furniture company and gives you some industry averages. He is trying to figure out what is going on.
prompt.question: Given the income statement and industry averages provided, what is going on with this company and what recommendations would you make?

clarifying_info.a: The client is primarily interested in maximizing profit.

clarifying_info.q: Why do furniture manufacturers have returns and allowances?
clarifying_info.a: If the retail furniture seller sees visible marks or tears on the furniture.

clarifying_info.q: Does our client have more expensive raw materials than the industry?
clarifying_info.a: No, they have similar raw materials costs to the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Does our client have more expensive labor costs than the industry?
clarifying_info.a: No, they have similar labor costs to the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Do the client's competitors have an economies of scale advantage?
clarifying_info.a: No, our client actually has the largest sales in the industry.

clarifying_info.q: Does our client have more expensive transportation costs?
clarifying_info.a: No, they have similar transportation costs.

clarifying_info.q: What market does the client serve?
clarifying_info.a: The medium-priced furniture segment — this does not include extremely expensive furniture; both client and competitors sell similar types of furniture.

clarifying_info.q: Who does our client typically sell furniture to?
clarifying_info.a: End customers are apartment dwellers and first-time home buyers. Immediately, 40% is sold to furniture stores and 60% through department stores where the client has exclusive arrangements. One department store accounts for 10% of all sales.

clarifying_info.q: Who do our client's competitors typically sell to?
clarifying_info.a: Same end customers. Competitors sell 90% to furniture stores and only 10% through department stores with exclusive arrangements.

clarifying_info.q: Are there price differences between the two customer segments?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — department stores typically demand a price break for the exclusive arrangement, or else they switch to a competitor. They have also been pushing for larger price breaks in recent years.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client sell to these different segments?
clarifying_info.a: They hire independent furniture salespeople to contract with each store.
They are paid a 5% commission based on Net Revenue.

clarifying_info.q: Do the salespeople have the ability to adjust the price?

exhibits.title: Income Statement with Industry Averages
exhibits.shows: The company's income statement alongside industry average benchmarks for key line items

framework: Start by benchmarking the income statement against industry averages to identify where the gaps are
Separate revenue issues from cost issues: check gross revenue, returns & allowances, and net revenue first, then move to COGS and SGA
Use Five Forces (particularly buyer power) to diagnose structural revenue problems
Investigate the sales channel mix — department stores vs. furniture stores — and the pricing dynamics in each
Examine the sales force incentive structure and its effect on pricing decisions
Assess balance sheet implications: zero interest expense signals no debt, raising questions about capital structure and acquisition risk

questions.prompt: Compare the client's income statement to industry averages. Where are the biggest gaps?
questions.guidance: COGS is 87% of net revenue vs. 80% industry average — a 7-point gap — and net profit is 2% vs. 10% industry average. Returns & allowances are 5% of gross revenue (600-570=30, 30/600=5%) vs. 2% industry average, indicating a 3-point overage. The primary drag is COGS, but returns are also elevated.

math.setup: Returns & Allowances = Gross Revenue - Net Revenue = 600 - 570 = 30; as % of Gross Revenue = 30/600
steps: COGS as % of Net Revenue = 496 / 570 = 87% — vs. industry 80%
Net Profit as % of Net Revenue = 11 / 570 = ~2% — vs. industry 10%
Gap in Net Profit = 10% - 2% = 8 percentage points, or ~$45.6M shortfall (8% × 570)
math.answer: Client lags industry by 7pp on COGS margin and 8pp on net profit margin; returns & allowances are 2.5× the industry rate.

questions.prompt: Given that raw materials, labor, transportation, and scale are all comparable to the industry, what is driving the COGS gap?
questions.guidance: Since all cost inputs are similar to the industry, the COGS gap is unlikely to be a pure cost problem. The candidate should pivot to revenue quality: the department store channel demands price discounts (lower net revenue per unit) while COGS remains the same, mechanically inflating COGS as a % of net revenue. The revenue-per-unit issue is the root cause.

questions.prompt: Diagnose the channel mix and buyer power issue using the Five Forces framework.
questions.guidance: Department stores represent 60% of client's sales vs. only 10% for competitors. Department stores use buyer power (exclusive arrangements, threat to switch) to extract price discounts. This lowers net revenue while costs remain flat, compressing margins. Competitors are insulated because they are far less dependent on department stores. This is the B-level answer: identifying buyer power as the root cause of poor profitability.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the sales force compensation structure and its contribution to the problem.
questions.guidance: Salespeople earn 5% commission on Net Revenue and have discretion to cut prices. This creates a misaligned incentive: reps maximize their commission by closing volume at discounted prices rather than protecting margin. On the single largest account (10% of sales = $60M net revenue), the rep earns 5% × $60M = $3M per year — an extremely high payout for one account, suggesting the company could internalize this role for that account and save most of that $3M.

math.setup: Largest account = 10% of Net Revenue = 10% × 570 = 57, rounding to $60M per casebook; commission = 5% × $60M
steps: 5% × $60M = $3M commission for one rep on one account
math.answer: The rep on the largest account earns ~$3M/year. Internalizing that account's sales role could recover most of this cost.

questions.prompt: What does the zero interest expense tell you about the company's situation?
questions.guidance: Zero interest means the company carries no debt and is entirely equity-financed. With a 2% net profit margin while the industry earns 10%, the company is significantly under-performing. Two implications: (1) adding debt/interest would push the company into losses; (2) an all-equity, under-performing company with the largest revenue in the industry is a potentially attractive acquisition or takeover target. This is the A+ insight.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to the CEO to improve profitability?

categories.name: Revenue / Pricing
ideas: Re-negotiate or exit department store exclusive arrangements that demand unsustainable price discounts
Gradually shift channel mix toward furniture stores (higher net revenue per unit), mirroring competitor distribution
Introduce tiered pricing floors — remove salespeople's authority to discount below a minimum margin threshold

categories.name: Sales Force Incentives
ideas: Restructure commission from % of Net Revenue to % of Gross Margin to align reps with profitability
Internalize the sales role for the top department store account (10% of sales, ~$60M) to capture the ~$3M commission
Consider moving to a hybrid model: salaried + smaller variable component tied to margin, not revenue

categories.name: Returns & Allowances
ideas: Investigate root causes of 5% returns vs. 2% industry — improve QC or packaging to reduce visible damage in transit
Introduce vendor-managed returns process to reduce allowances given to department stores

categories.name: Strategic / Capital Structure
ideas: Explore adding debt financing to fund growth or buybacks, improving ROE for equity holders
Conduct defensive review of takeover vulnerability given all-equity structure and below-industry margins
Consider whether department store channel can be restructured into a direct-to-consumer or online channel to improve pricing control

recommendation: The primary problem is a revenue issue, not a cost issue: department stores (60% of sales) are using buyer power to extract price discounts, which inflates COGS as a % of net revenue and compresses margins to 2% vs. 10% industry average
Immediately restructure salesperson incentives from % of Net Revenue to % of Gross Margin, and internalize the sales function for the largest department store account to recover ~$3M in commission
Medium-term, rebalance the channel mix away from department stores toward furniture stores to reduce buyer power exposure and improve pricing quality
risks: Department stores may respond to renegotiation by switching to competitors, causing a near-term revenue decline
Internalizing the salesforce adds fixed cost and management complexity
The company's all-equity, under-performing profile makes it a potential acquisition target — management should be aware of this vulnerability
next_steps: Analyze profitability by channel (furniture stores vs. each department store) to quantify the margin drag from discounting
Model the revenue/profit trade-off of reducing department store share by 10–20pp over 2–3 years
Design a new compensation plan tied to gross margin and pilot with 2–3 reps before full rollout
Brief the board on takeover risk and consider defensive options
